facts.fact: Planaria are free-living flatworms about 5–15 mm long. They glide along surfaces and are mostly active at night.
Planaria eat shrimp eggs and shrimplets of 1–3 mm, and may attack weak or freshly moulted shrimp.
Planaria attack baby shrimp, sick shrimp and shrimp that have just moulted, and they also compete with shrimp for food and space.
Hydra are freshwater cnidarians, related to jellyfish, corals and sea anemones. They have a stalk or foot and a mouth ringed by tentacles with stinging cells.
Hydra can regenerate from fragments and reproduce by budding, or sexually by eggs.
Adult shrimp are generally safe from hydra, but newborn shrimplets of about 2–3 mm are easy targets. A hydra infestation can sharply cut survival in a breeding tank within days.
Baby shrimp are vulnerable to hydra because their shells are still soft and they fit in a hydra's mouth. Old or sick adult shrimp may occasionally be stung.
Hydra are not dangerous to humans because their stinging cells are too weak.
Aquarium Co-Op's author, writing from experience, says hydra do not greatly reduce populations of baby fish and shrimp.
Planaria have an arrow- or triangle-shaped head with two dark eyespots.
Planaria are flat, unsegmented and glide smoothly. Detritus worms are round in cross-section, segmented, wriggle actively and are harmless decomposers.
Head shape alone is not a reliable way to identify planaria. Combine several features and get a clear close-up photo before treating.
Planaria can be white, off-white or rust/brown-red, so color alone does not identify them.
Rhabdocoela flatworms have rounded heads and tails, are harmless to shrimp, and often gather on the glass when the lights are off.
Rhabdocoela (tiny, round-headed) and detritus worms are harmless and do not need treatment.
Planaria are basically white, but their color can change with the food they eat.
A warning sign of planaria is berried female shrimp that never produce surviving young.
Hydra look like small translucent stalks with tentacles, usually 5–15 mm long, attached to glass, plants, hardscape and equipment.
Hydra grow up to about 1 cm (0.4 in) and are translucent white, green or light brown.
ShrimpScience says fully grown hydra reach about 3 cm and look like a stick with jellyfish-like tentacles. They are usually white but can be lime green.
Green hydra (Hydra viridissima) get their color from symbiotic Chlorella algae.
Gensou names the two common aquarium hydra as green hydra (H. vulgaris) and brown hydra (H. oligactis).
Planaria enter tanks on contaminated plants, substrate and driftwood, in live food such as blackworms and tubifex, and on shared nets, siphons or water from infested tanks.
Overfeeding is the main driver of planaria population explosions.
At 28–32 °C, a few planaria can become hundreds within weeks.
Excess organic matter, overfeeding and poor substrate maintenance favor planaria. Their egg capsules are nearly invisible on plants and decorations.
Leftover high-protein food encourages planaria. Plants, fish or water bought from shops that already carry them, and poor-quality substrate, can bring them in.
Hydra arrive on new plants and driftwood and in water from fish bags. Overfeeding feeds the copepods, daphnia and detritus worms that hydra eat.
Hydra can lie dormant for months, then bloom when baby brine shrimp are fed heavily.
Overfeeding powdered food favors hydra, and sharing nets or equipment between tanks spreads them.
Cutting back feeding and doing water changes is shrimp-safe and always the first step against planaria, but it is not enough for an established infestation.
A few hydra are not an emergency, but numbers should be kept low.
If shrimp show severe stress during planaria treatment, do a 50% water change immediately.
No Planaria (areca/betel nut extract): 1 scoop (included) per 50 L, or as the product label instructs. It is shrimp-safe at the recommended dose.
Gensou's planaria guide says snails are generally safe with No Planaria, but suggests starting at half dose if valuable snails are present.
Gensou's hydra guide says snails are highly sensitive to No Planaria, so remove nerite, ramshorn and Malaysian trumpet snails first.
Some Caridina keepers see mild stress with No Planaria. Gensou suggests a 20% lower dose for crystal red and Taiwan bee shrimp.
Shrimp-safe does not mean snail-safe. Follow the exact label of No Planaria and remove snails first.
Fenbendazole for planaria: 0.1 g pure fenbendazole per 100 L, or about 0.45 g Safeguard granules (22.2%) per 100 L, pre-mixed in warm dechlorinated water. It is lethal to snails.
Fenbendazole for hydra: 0.1 g per 40 L dissolved in warm water. Hydra die within 48–72 hours, and it is shrimp-safe at the correct dose.
After 72 hours of fenbendazole, do a 50% water change, put the carbon back and siphon out dead hydra. Repeat the dose a week later for survivors.
Aquarium Co-Op uses Safe-Guard goat dewormer (10% fenbendazole, 100 mg/ml) at 1 drop per gallon, shaken well. It works within 24 hours. After 3 days, do a 50% water change and redose if needed.
Aquarium Co-Op reports that, in its experience, the Safe-Guard dose was safe for snails, shrimp, fish, plants and beneficial bacteria (anecdotal).
PVAS says half a drop per gallon of SafeGuard fenbendazole liquid is enough for hydra. High concentrations can kill fish, so err on the low side.
Wait at least 3 days and do a 50% water change before repeating a fenbendazole dose.
Panacur C (fenbendazole) is a dog dewormer used off-label. Its label does not establish an aquarium dose or safety for shrimp and snails, so Superior Shrimp advises seeking aquatic veterinary advice.
After fenbendazole, ShrimpScience's author lost Malaysian trumpet snails, and ramshorn snails kept dying for months. It took about a year before the tank was safe for snails again.
Hydra treatments usually harm snails, because snails are biologically similar to hydra.
Other hydra and planaria products named include Planaria Zero and SL-Aqua Bio Protector Z1.
Salt is not a viable planaria treatment in shrimp tanks.
Bait traps reduce planaria numbers but cannot wipe out an infestation alone. They also miss eggs and planaria living under the substrate.
Planaria trap: put raw meat, shrimp or fish in a small container covered by fine mesh with a central hole. Set it overnight and remove it in the morning.
Loaches and puffers eat planaria but are not compatible with shrimp tanks.
Honey gourami and sparkling gourami eat hydra over a few days, but sparkling gouramis will also eat shrimplets.
Physa pond snails sometimes eat hydra, but results are inconsistent, so use them only as a supplement.
Aquarium Co-Op says ramshorn, pond and spixi snails eat hydra and are too slow to catch fry or shrimp.
Spixi snails eat hydra but do not clear them quickly.
Starving hydra by reducing food (target feeding, feeding dishes, water changes, gravel vacuuming) makes most of them die off.
Manual removal of hydra: siphon them with a syringe and airline tubing. Removing only some lets them regrow within days.

Planaria protocol, day 0: change 20% of the water, remove activated carbon and chemical media, measure the real water volume, remove snails (if using fenbendazole), turn off UV, dose, and add a little more surface agitation.
Days 1–2: dead planaria show up as white curled worms. Shrimp may be less active but should still move and feed.
Day 3: give a second dose at the same concentration. Days 5–6: give an optional third dose, recommended for heavy infestations.
Day 7: do a 50% water change matching temperature and TDS, vacuum dead worms, put the carbon back and turn UV on again.
After treatment, test ammonia and nitrite daily for a week. Planaria eggs can take up to two weeks to hatch, so check nightly with a torch.
Treatment counts as successful if no planaria are seen for two consecutive weeks, starting from week 4.
After hydra treatment, use carbon or Purigen to remove leftover medication. Test ammonia, nitrite and TDS for a week, and wait at least two weeks before adding new livestock.
Quarantine new plants for 1–2 weeks and inspect them, or use tissue-culture plants.
Alum dip for new plants: 1 tablespoon potassium alum per litre for 2–3 hours, then rinse thoroughly.
Feed only what shrimp eat within two hours and remove leftovers promptly.
Feed solid foods such as pellets or algae wafers instead of powdered food, and use a feeding dish.
Boil and scrub new hardscape, and do not share nets or equipment between tanks.
Get live food from well-maintained cultures and do not transfer the culture water or debris.
No quarantine period or peroxide dip is guaranteed to remove every worm or egg capsule.
Leaving carbon in the filter while dosing, which lowers effectiveness.
Stopping after one or two doses, which lets surviving eggs hatch later.
Working out the dose without subtracting the water displaced by substrate, hardscape and equipment.
Ignoring hardscape displacement causes overdosing: dosing for 40 L when the tank holds 30 L is about a 30% overdose.
Assuming every small white worm is planaria, and treating before confirming identification.
Using a dosing schedule from another brand or an old guide, or converting a dog dose into a tank dose.
Using a live snail to test whether treatment residue is gone.
Scraping hydra off by hand is not advised, because broken fragments regrow.
Leaving dead worms in the tank after treatment, which risks ammonia spikes.
Vietnamese shrimp keepers use the Z1 planaria remover, which tepcanh.com says does not harm shrimp or plants but does affect snails.
Vietnamese folk remedies for planaria include starfruit (khế), dried areca nut (cau khô), soap pod (bồ kết) and lemongrass (sả). tepcanh.com notes these are unverified.
Products sold in Vietnam include Genchem No Planaria and Bio S Planaria Killer. BucepViet advises using half the recommended No Planaria dose in shrimp tanks.
BucepViet advises changing 50% of the water with RO water 48 hours after medicating a shrimp tank, and adding beneficial bacteria about 2 days after treatment.
Raising the temperature to 30–32 °C against worms should not be done in shrimp tanks.
In tropical water of 28–32 °C, organic matter breaks down fast, so careful feeding matters more.
Superior Shrimp says ramshorn snails are not a proven treatment for planaria or a barrier against them.
ShrimpScience says green hydra cannot be starved easily, because their algae feed them.
Superior Shrimp says frozen food is not a guarantee against bringing in aquatic pests.
Superior Shrimp says a quick dip, a fixed waiting period or clear water does not prove eggs are gone or that the tank is safe for snails.
